value.overview: The Volcano Hummingbird (Selasphorus flammula) is a tiny hummingbird of the highest mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is especially associated with páramo, stunted high-elevation woodland, shrublands, and open areas near the tree line. Males show striking regional variation in throat color, while females are mostly green above and pale below with a spotted or lightly marked throat. The species is well adapted to cool, windy mountain environments.
value.classification: The Volcano Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Selasphorus. Three geographically separated subspecies are commonly recognized: flammula, simoni, and torridus.
value.identification: This is a very small, compact hummingbird with a short, straight bill, green upperparts, and a dark, somewhat forked tail. Adult males have a glittering gorget whose color varies among mountain ranges, including reddish, pinkish, purplish, or grayish tones. Females and immature birds lack the bold male throat and show pale underparts with dusky spotting. Its tiny size and high-elevation range help distinguish it from larger mountain hummingbirds, although it can resemble the related Scintillant Hummingbird.
value.rangeHabitat: The Volcano Hummingbird occurs in Costa Rica and extends into extreme western Panama around Volcán Barú. In Costa Rica it is a characteristic resident of the Cordillera Volcánica Central, including the high mountains around Poás, Barva, Irazú, and Turrialba, and of the Cordillera de Talamanca, including high peaks such as Cerro de la Muerte and Chirripó. It uses páramo, subpáramo, elfin and dwarf woodland, shrubby clearings, forest edges, landslide openings, volcanic disturbance areas, and high-elevation gardens.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals make local or seasonal altitudinal movements, sometimes descending from the highest páramo and exposed mountain slopes to lower montane edges during unfavorable weather or outside the breeding season.
value.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly during the wetter part of the year, with timing varying among mountain regions. The female builds a very small cup-shaped nest from plant fibers, down, moss, lichen, and spider web, usually placed on a shrub or small tree and often sheltered by overhanging vegetation. She incubates the eggs and raises the young alone. Nest placement may occur along forest edges, steep slopes, trails, or shrubby highland clearings.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of nectar from small high-elevation flowers, supplemented by tiny insects and other arthropods. It forages by hovering at flowers and may also take insects in short aerial sallies. In Costa Rica it visits flowering shrubs and plants in páramo, montane scrub, forest edges, disturbed clearings, and suitable gardens. Its ability to use scattered flowers is important in the open, windy habitats of the upper mountains.
value.behavior: Volcano Hummingbirds are active and quick, often moving rapidly between flowers and perches. They are commonly seen alone and may defend productive flower patches from other hummingbirds. Males perform brief displays and aerial chases, especially around feeding areas or during courtship. Birds often perch on exposed twigs or low shrubs, where their small size and subdued female plumage can make them difficult to detect despite their bright, flashing gorgets.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable.
